title: client-side-socket-leak-and-dns-cache-scratchpad
content:
Purpose:
Quick personal scratchpad for an ongoing private-deploy networking flake that looks like a mix of ephemeral socket exhaustion, DNS fallback behavior, and intermittent TLS handshake failures when clients call external APIs from on-prem nodes through the customer egress/NAT stack.

Summary of symptoms (as seen by app processes on private nodes):
- Random ~1-3% of outbound requests to external vendor endpoints (api.example-cdn.com) fail with TLS handshake errors: TLS alert, unexpected_message / handshake_failure in client logs. Failures are transient (succeed on retry a few seconds later).
- Long tail of sockets in TIME_WAIT and CLOSE_WAIT on some nodes after bursts. System metrics show FD consumption spikes aligned with request spikes.
- Intermittent DNS resolution fallback to internal stub resolver (169.254.169.253) seen in strace/ldns logs. Some queries appear to time out and then succeed via a different resolver.
- No obvious packet drops on egress NAT gateway metrics; NAT gateway reports normal throughput.

Hypotheses (ranked):
1) Local ephemeral port exhaustion + TIME_WAIT accumulation causes delayed connection attempts or weird port reuse leading to TLS server rejecting resume (SNI mismatch or early data issues).
2) conntrack table pressure leading to dropped/garbled connections (server sees a half-open flow).
3) Fragmentation/MTU interaction causing ClientHello truncation for some packets (handshake failures) on certain path MTU sizes (we saw similar with heavy MTU manipulations previously).
4) DNS resolver ordering fallbacks cause requests to go to a different egress path (peered vs transit) and that path has different TLS-terminating middleboxes (WAF/load-balancer) that reject some TLS variants.
5) Kernel TCP settings (TCP_TFO, tcp_tw_reuse, tcp_tw_recycle behavior) interacting with upstream NAT and TLS session resumption.

Observations and notes from first-pass checks (commands run on affected node ip-10-1-5-12):
- ss -s 
  Total: 12005 (kernel); TCP: 9000 (estab 8400, closed 300)
  TIME-WAIT: 1500  (unusually high for baseline ~200)
- ss -tnp | grep api.example-cdn.com | wc -l -> ~40 at sampling (many ephemeral, but not huge)
- netstat -anp | grep TIME_WAIT | head -n 5
  tcp 0 0 10.1.5.12:52346 34.210.45.99:443 TIME_WAIT -
  tcp 0 0 10.1.5.12:52350 34.210.45.99:443 TIME_WAIT -
- conntrack -L | egrep "ESTABLISHED|SYN_SENT" | wc -l -> 8200 (conntrack_max is 65536, so comfortably below)
- cat /proc/sys/net/ipv4/ip_local_port_range -> 32768 60999 (default-ish)
- ss -o state time-wait shows typical timers ~60s

TLS-specific checks (from app container logs + tcpdump):
- App logs show: "tls: client handshake failed: tls: unexpected message"
- tcpdump -nni eth0 host 34.210.45.99 and port 443 captured several ClientHellos followed by RST from remote IP (rare) or nothing.
- Extracted first ClientHello for a failing case (wireshark): length fields looked normal, but some packets for the ClientHello were fragmented across two IP fragments (we have DF set off?), causing reassembly on path?
- strace -e trace=network myapp: timeouts on connect(2) occasionally return EADDRNOTAVAIL after many sockets opened quickly (possible ephemeral port exhaustion).

DNS behavior:
- dig +short @127.0.0.53 api.example-cdn.com -> 34.210.45.99
- dig +short @169.254.169.253 api.example-cdn.com -> 52.23.1.14 (different IP)
- /etc/resolv.conf using stub resolver systemd-resolved (127.0.0.53) with fallback to customers' recursive resolvers via peering. Observed a period where the stub resolver returned SERVFAIL rapidly and the app retried directly against 169.254.169.253 (configured by on-prem edge).

Customer network topology points (confirmed with infra):
- Node -> on-prem router (AS65020) -> peering -> cloud transit gateway -> NAT/firewall -> internet.
- There is an SDA appliance that does TLS inspection for some domains (only for certain resolved IP ranges).
- Path to 34.210.45.99 is via peered transit A (low-latency). Path to 52.23.1.14 goes via transit B where TLS inspection is in-line.

Commands tried (and results):
- curl -v --tlsv1.3 --ciphers TLS_AES_128_GCM_SHA256 https://api.example-cdn.com/health
  -> sometimes completes; failing case: "* SSL peer connection reset" then "curl: (56) Received HTTP code 0 from server"
- curl with --tls-max 1.2 -> works consistently in one failing window (suggests server/proxy has trouble with TLS 1.3 handshake variants).
- curl --interface 10.1.5.12 to force source IP -- identical behavior depending on resolver IP chosen.
- sudo sysctl -w net.ipv4.tcp_tw_reuse=1 (temporary test): reduced TIME_WAIT counts but didn't eliminate handshake errors.
- disabled TFO (tcp_fastopen) on node and worker pod runtime -> no significant change.
- iptables -t nat -L -n showed standard MASQUERADE rules for outbound, no obvious rate-limiting chains.
- tcpdump captured a failing connection where ClientHello was sent, then an RST from an intermediate IP (likely inspection appliance) 203.0.113.17. Packet shows TLS extension with early_data present on the ClientHello. When we disabled early_data on the client, failures dropped.

Interim conclusions so far:
- There is a combination of path-dependent middleboxes (TLS inspection appliance) and some client behavior (early_data/0-RTT, TLS 1.3) that triggers the appliance into resetting the connection. The resolver fallback changing IPs exposes calls to different intermediate devices.
- TIME_WAIT pileups and ephemeral exhaustion exacerbate the surface area (more concurrent fresh connections -> more early_data attempts and more flow interactions).

Immediate mitigation options tried and notes: 
- Disabled 0-RTT/early_data in the client library (patch): reduced failure rate by ~85% in canary. Reverted for further testing after acceptance.
- Increased ephemeral port range and lowered tcp_tw_lifetime to 30s for canary nodes: reduced EADDRNOTAVAIL occurrences.
- Force resolver to use the preferred path (bypass 169.254 fallback) by pinning a static DNS entry in hosts for critical vendor domain during incident (temporary, manual).

Longer-term remediation items (proposed):
- Work with customer network team to map exact ACL/inspection behavior for vendor IP ranges and update resolver ordering or routing to avoid the inspection path for this vendor.
- Add a connection-level feature flag in SDKs to disable early_data for on-prem cluster mode by default until we negotiate inspection compatibility.
- Update cluster default kernel params for ephemeral ports and timewait heuristics in private-deploy docs; bake into cloud-init for private nodes.
- Add targeted metrics: count of TLS early_data attempts, per-destination resolver path used, and per-node fd exhaustion alerts.

Notes for reproducing locally (dev node steps):
1) Setup small VM on same peered transit or simulate with netem to create two different egress paths (we used two NATV4 mocks).
2) Run a client with early_data enabled and repeated parallel requests (100 concurrent) to vendor domain. Observe rate of failures.
3) Toggle resolver to return alternate IP and observe failure delta.

Loose todo & next experiments:
- [ ] Run full conntrack stress test to see behavior when conntrack table approaches limits (increase ephemeral connections, check for NAT timeouts).
- [ ] Capture pcap across both sides of peering point (ask infra for mirror) to see where ClientHello is mutilated or reset.
- [ ] Coordinate with vendor ops to get debug logs on failing handshakes (SNI seen, TLS version, early_data flag). Ticketed: JIRA-INC-7891.
- [ ] Add an agent-side feature toggle to disable 0-RTT in SDKs for private-deploy customers and test rollout.
- [ ] Consider configuring systemd-resolved stub resolver to prefer customer resolver (avoid fallback to management resolver) via DHCP options.

Open questions / unknowns:
- Is the inspection appliance sensitive to TLS extension ordering or to early_data specifically? (need vendor logs)
- Why did some nodes show much higher TIME_WAIT counts than others under identical traffic? Possible difference in client library versions or kernel tunables on those nodes.
- Could a NAT device be rewriting sequence numbers or doing something that breaks reassembly (we saw fragmenting of ClientHello)?

Slack snippets and quick references:
- slack:#private-deploy "Ava: saw 0-RTT causing resets, pinning DNS avoided path B" (2026-03-03)
- github PR: github.com/redwood-inference/private-deploy/pull/458 (temp SDK toggle to disable early_data)

If/when we close this: document default behavior in private-deploy onboarding and include recommended kernel params and SDK defaults to avoid footguns with middlebox-rich customer networks.

End of scratchpad.
